terms.grammar: verb phrase, intransitive; often impersonal (nōn successit, it didn’t work)
evidence: Ter. And. 670: Hāc nōn successit, aliā aggrediēmur viā.
Cic. Or. 98 (Lewis & Short): sī quandō minus succēdet
terms.comment: Of a plan or an attempt: nōn successit, it didn’t work; minus succēdit, it isn’t going well (Lewis & Short s.v. succēdō).

terms.gloss: fail, fall flat (of a play); fail (an exam)
evidence: Hor. Epist. 2.1.176: sēcūrus cadat an rēctō stet fābula tālō
terms.comment: Of a play that fails on the stage, the opposite of stāre (Lewis & Short); hence Traupman’s “fail an exam”. Morgan–Owens (s.v. fail) suggests, with a query, the passive improbārī, to be failed.

evidence: Phaedr. 1.26.10: quae cum lagōnae collum frūstrā lamberet
terms.comment: With a verb of trying it says that the attempt failed: frūstrā cōnātus est. As a cry, “missed!” (see miss).

evidence: Caes. BG 7.20 (Lewis & Short): sī nihil in oppugnātiōne oppidī prōfēcisset
Liv. 2.6 (Lewis & Short): spēs ad irritum cadēns

terms.gloss: be turned down (for a post, in an election)

phrases.latin: Dēceptus sum, at nōn dēfatīgātus. … Hāc nōn successit, aliā aggrediēmur viā.
phrases.english: I’ve been foiled, but I’m not worn out… That way didn’t work; we’ll go at it another way.

phrases.latin: gestit enim nummum in loculōs dēmittere, post hoc sēcūrus cadat an rēctō stet fābula tālō
phrases.english: For he is eager to drop the money into his purse; after that he does not care whether his play falls flat or stands firm on its feet.

phrases.latin: quae cum lagōnae collum frūstrā lamberet, peregrīnam sīc locūtam volucrem accēpimus: sua quisque exempla dēbet aequō animō patī
phrases.english: As the fox licked the neck of the jar in vain, the stranger bird, so we are told, said: “Everyone should bear patiently being treated as he treats others.”
to fail an exam (a test, a quiz)
